title: Doubly linked list: build, print, insert, delete
overview: A doubly linked list gives every node two links: `next` to the node after it and `prev` to the node before it. This module builds one by hand, prints it both ways, and writes insert and delete at the head, the tail and any index. The extra `prev` link makes tail deletion O(1) and backward walks easy, but every operation now has two links to keep correct.

concepts.explain: Each node stores `val`, `next` and `prev`. The constructor sets both links to `NULL` so a new node is not connected to anything yet.
concepts.snippet: class Node { public: int val; Node* next; Node* prev; };

concepts.explain: `head->prev` and `tail->next` are both `NULL`. Keeping a `tail` pointer lets you start at either end.
Forward: start at `head` and follow `next`. Backward: start at `tail` and follow `prev`. No recursion needed.
concepts.snippet: for(Node* t = tail; t; t = t->prev) cout << t->val << " ";

concepts.explain: If `A->next == B`, then `B->prev` must be `A`. Each insert or delete must fix both directions, or forward and backward prints will disagree.

concepts.term: Insert in the middle: four links
concepts.explain: To put `newNode` after `tmp`: point `newNode->next` at `tmp->next`, point `tmp->next->prev` back at `newNode`, then `tmp->next = newNode` and `newNode->prev = tmp`.
Thanks to `prev`, the new tail is simply `tail->prev`; no walk from the head is needed.
concepts.snippet: tail = tail->prev; delete tail->next; tail->next = NULL;

concepts.explain: Index 0 is a head operation; the last position is a tail operation; a one-node list must set both `head` and `tail` to `NULL` when emptied.

files.title: Build a doubly linked list by hand
files.what: Creates three nodes (10, 20, 30) and wires both `next` and `prev` links manually. It prints nothing; it only shows the structure.
steps: `head` = 10, `a` = 20, `tail` = 30, all with `NULL` links.
`head->next = a` and `a->prev = head` connect 10 and 20 both ways.
`a->next = tail` and `tail->prev = a` connect 20 and 30 both ways.
files.output_note: No output — the program only builds the list.

check.q: How many link assignments are needed to connect three nodes both ways?
check.a: Four: two `next` links and two `prev` links.

files.title: Build a doubly linked list (practice copy)
files.what: Identical re-typing of the manual setup.
steps: Same three nodes and four link assignments.
files.output_note: No output.

check.q: What is `head->prev` in this list?
check.a: `NULL` — nothing comes before the head.

files.title: Print forward and backward
files.what: Prints the hand-built list from head to tail using `next`, then from tail to head using `prev`.
steps: `print_forward` starts at `head` and follows `tmp->next` until `NULL`.
`print_backward` starts at `tail` and follows `tmp->prev` until `NULL`.
Each function ends its line with `endl`.
files.output_note: `10 20 30` then `30 20 10` — the same nodes read in both directions.

check.q: What does a singly linked list need to print backward that a doubly linked list does not?
check.a: Recursion (or an extra stack), because it has no `prev` links.

files.title: Print both ways (practice copy)
files.what: Re-typed version with a constructor bug that leaves the links uninitialised.
steps: Same two print functions, but `print_forward` no longer ends its line.
files.output_note: `10 20 30` followed by an endless run of garbage numbers, until the run times out: the tail's `next` is not `NULL`, so the walk wanders through random memory.
files.watch_out: The constructor says `this->next = next; this->prev = prev;` — the members are assigned to themselves and stay garbage. Use `NULL` for both. The missing `cout << endl;` in `print_forward` would also glue the two lines together.

check.q: Which node's link actually caused the endless print?
check.a: `tail->next`, which was never set to `NULL`.

files.title: Read a doubly linked list from input (buggy)
files.what: Meant to read values until -1 with `insert_at_tail` and print the list, but `main` exits before printing.
steps: `insert_at_tail` links the new node after `tail` (`tail->next = newNode`, `newNode->prev = tail`) and moves `tail`.
The loop reads values and appends them.
On -1 the code runs `return;` — this leaves `main` entirely, so `print_forward` is never reached.
files.output_note: Empty output: the program ends as soon as it reads -1. After the fix it prints `10 20 30`.
files.watch_out: Use `break;` instead of `return;` inside the loop. (A bare `return;` in `int main` is also not valid C++; the compiler here only accepts it with `-fpermissive`.)

check.q: What is the difference between `break` and `return` inside that loop?
check.a: `break` leaves only the loop; `return` leaves the whole function, skipping everything after it.

files.title: Read a doubly linked list (practice copy)
files.what: Identical copy, including the `return;` bug.
steps: Same input loop that exits `main` on -1.
files.output_note: Empty output, for the same reason as the original.

check.q: Why is `insert_at_tail` O(1) in a doubly linked list with a `tail` pointer?
check.a: It only touches the current tail and the new node — no walking.

files.title: Insert at the head
files.what: Adds 100 in front of the list 10 20 30.
steps: If the list is empty, the new node becomes both `head` and `tail`.
Otherwise `newNode->next = head` links forward.
`head->prev = newNode` links the old head back.
`head = newNode` makes it the first node.

check.q: Which link is new compared with inserting at the head of a singly list?
check.a: `head->prev = newNode`.

files.title: Insert at the head (practice copy)
files.what: Same code, inserting 5 instead of 100.
steps: Same three-link head insert.

check.q: After this insert, what is `head->next->prev->val`?
check.a: 5 — the new head.

files.title: Insert at the tail
files.what: Appends 100 twice to the end of 10 20 30.
steps: Empty list: the new node is both `head` and `tail`.
Otherwise `tail->next = newNode` and `newNode->prev = tail`.
Move `tail = newNode`.

check.q: Why must `tail` be passed by reference?
check.a: The function moves `tail` to the new node, and the caller must see that change.

files.title: Insert at the tail (practice copy)
files.what: Same code, appending 40 and then 50.
steps: Same tail insert.

check.q: What does `print_backward(tail)` print at the end?

files.title: Insert at any index
files.what: Inserts values at index 2, index 0 and index 5, reusing the head and tail inserts for the edge cases.
steps: `pos == 0` → call `insert_at_head` and return.
Otherwise walk `tmp` to index `pos-1`.
If `tmp` is the last node (`tmp->next == NULL`), call `insert_at_tail`.
Otherwise wire the four links: `newNode->next`, `tmp->next->prev`, `tmp->next`, `newNode->prev`.
files.output_note: Each line shows the list after one operation. Line 4 has 200 at index 2, line 5 has 300 at index 0, and line 6 has 400 at index 5 (after 30).
files.watch_out: `newNode` is created before the edge-case checks, so in the head and tail cases it is never used and leaks. Create it after those checks. There is also no check that `pos` is within `0..size`.

check.q: In the middle case, why set `tmp->next->prev` before changing `tmp->next`?
check.a: After `tmp->next = newNode`, you can no longer reach the old next node through `tmp`.

files.title: Insert at any index (practice copy)
files.what: Same functions with a shorter demo: one tail insert, then 200 at index 2, 500 at index 0 and 600 at index 6 (the end).
steps: Index 6 equals the list size, so the walk stops on the last node and `insert_at_tail` is used.
files.output_note: Last line `500 10 20 200 30 100 600` — 600 went to the very end.

check.q: For a list of size 6, which insert indexes are valid?
check.a: 0 through 6 (6 means append at the tail).

files.title: Delete the head
files.what: After the insert demo, removes the first node twice.
steps: Empty list → return.
One node → delete it and set `tail = NULL`.
Otherwise save `head`, move `head = head->next`, set `head->prev = NULL`, and delete the saved node.
files.output_note: The last two lines lose 300 and then 10 from the front: `10 20 200 30 400 100 100`, then `20 200 30 400 100 100`.
files.watch_out: In the one-node case `head` is deleted but not set to `NULL`, so it becomes a dangling pointer. Add `head = NULL;` (the practice copy does).

check.q: Why set `head->prev = NULL` after moving `head`?
check.a: Otherwise the new head still points back at the freed node.

files.title: Delete the head (practice copy)
files.what: Same program with the one-node case fixed: it also sets `head = NULL`.
steps: Same head delete, now safe when the last node is removed.
files.output_note: Same lines as the original.

check.q: When the only node is deleted, what should `head` and `tail` be?
check.a: Both `NULL`.

files.title: Delete the tail
files.what: Removes the last node three times, using `prev` to find the new tail instantly.
steps: Save `tail` in `deleteNode`.
If `head == tail` (one node), delete it and set both to `NULL`.
Otherwise `tail = tail->prev` and `tail->next = NULL`.
Delete the saved node.
files.output_note: The last three lines lose one value from the end each time: `20 200 30 400 100`, `20 200 30 400`, `20 200 30`.
files.watch_out: It does not check for an empty list; calling it when `tail` is `NULL` crashes.

check.q: Why is this O(1) when the singly version was O(n)?
check.a: `tail->prev` gives the second-last node directly.

files.title: Delete the tail (practice copy)
files.what: Same result, but it cuts the link first with `tail->prev->next = NULL` and then moves `tail`.
steps: Both orders work, as long as `deleteNode` was saved first.
files.output_note: Same lines as the original.

check.q: Why is it safe to change `tail` before deleting?
check.a: The old tail is still reachable through `deleteNode`.

files.title: Delete at any index (crashes)
files.what: Deletes the node at a given index, using the head and tail deletes for the edge cases. The tail check is wrong, so the demo crashes.
steps: `pos == 0` → `delete_at_head`.
Walk `tmp` to index `pos-1`.
The code checks `tmp->next == NULL` to decide on a tail delete.
Otherwise unlink: `tmp->next = tmp->next->next`, then `tmp->next->prev = tmp`, and delete the saved node.
files.output_note: Output stops after `20 200 30` and the program crashes (access violation). Deleting index 2 removes the last node, so `tmp->next` becomes `NULL` and `tmp->next->prev` dereferences `NULL`.
files.watch_out: The tail test must look one node further: `if(tmp->next->next == NULL) { delete_at_tail(head, tail); return; }`. The practice copy has exactly this fix.

check.q: When `pos` is the last index, where does `tmp` stop?
check.a: On the second-last node, so `tmp->next` is the tail and `tmp->next->next` is `NULL`.

files.title: Delete at any index (fixed practice copy)
files.what: Same program with two fixes: the tail case checks `tmp->next->next == NULL`, and the one-node head delete sets `head = NULL`.
steps: Deleting the last index now goes to `delete_at_tail`, so no `NULL` is dereferenced.
files.output_note: Runs to the end: `20 200` (index 2 removed), `20 300 200`, `20 400 300 200`. The final delete has no print after it.

check.q: What list remains after the last `delete_at_any_position(head, tail, 2)`?
check.a: `20 400 200` — 300 at index 2 is removed.

files.title: All operations together (buggy main)
files.what: Collects all the doubly linked list functions in one file; `main` is supposed to read a list and print it, but the loop never runs.
steps: Contains `print_forward`, `print_backward`, the three inserts and the three deletes from this module.
`main` starts with `tail = NULL` and loops `while(tail)`.
Because `tail` is `NULL`, the loop body never runs, and nothing is read.
`print_forward(NULL)` prints just an empty line.
files.complexity: Time O(n) for input once fixed · Space O(n)
files.output_note: Just a blank line — no values were read. Once fixed it prints `10 20 30`.
files.watch_out: Use `while(true)` and `break;` on -1 (the current `return;` would also skip the print). The file also still has the `tmp->next == NULL` tail-check bug in `delete_at_any_position`.

check.q: Why does `while(tail)` never run here?
check.a: `tail` starts as `NULL`, which counts as false.

files.title: Design browser history (practice)
files.what: One browser tab as a doubly linked list of pages: `prev` is the page behind you, `next` the page ahead, and a single `current` pointer says where you are. `visit` adds a page, `back` and `forward` just move `current`.
steps: The `Node` is the module's doubly linked node with a `string url` instead of a number.

`visit(url)` links the new page after `current` and moves `current` onto it. That one link is also what drops the forward history: nothing points at the old `current->next` any more, so those pages can never be reached again.
`back(steps)` walks `current = current->prev` while there are steps left **and** a page behind; `forward` does the same along `next`.
Both return `current->url` after the walk, so running out of history is not an error - you simply stop at the end.
`main` reads the home page, a command count, then lines like `visit google.com`, `back 1`, `forward 2`, and prints what each back/forward returns.
files.complexity: Time O(1) per visit, O(steps) per back/forward · Space O(number of pages kept)
files.input:
leetcode.com
10
visit google.com
visit facebook.com
visit youtube.com
back 1
back 1
forward 1
visit linkedin.com
forward 2
back 2
back 7
files.input_note: Home page, then 10 commands - LeetCode's own example written in this command form.
files.output_note: Six lines, one per back/forward: `facebook.com`, `google.com`, `facebook.com`, then `linkedin.com` (nothing ahead after a visit, so `forward 2` stays put), `google.com`, and `leetcode.com` (`back 7` runs out of history and stops at the home page).
files.watch_out: The two guards in each loop are the whole problem. Without `current->prev != NULL`, `back(7)` walks off the front and crashes; without the `steps > 0` test you would always jump to the end.

check.q: After `visit`, why can you no longer go forward to the pages you had visited before?
check.a: `current->next` now points at the new page, so nothing points at the old chain and it is unreachable.

files.title: Flatten a multilevel doubly linked list (practice)

problem.name: LeetCode 430 - Flatten a Multilevel Doubly Linked List

files.what: Each node has the usual `val`, `next` and `prev` plus one extra link, `child`, which may point at another list. Every child list is spliced into the main chain right after the node that owned it, until the whole thing is one flat doubly linked list with no `child` left.
steps: Walk the list with `cur`. If `cur->child` is `NULL` there is nothing to do, just step on.
Otherwise save `cur->next` (the rest of this level) first - the next line overwrites it and those nodes would be unreachable.
Set `cur->child = NULL` straight away: the answer must have no child links left.
Link the child head after `cur` in both directions, then walk to the end of the child chain.
Attach the saved rest of the level after that end, fixing its `prev` too (unless it is `NULL`).
Step on with `cur = cur->next`, which now enters the child chain. Any children *inside* it are met later by the same loop, so one pass handles any depth.
`main` builds the list from a bracketed line and prints the result forward and backward.
files.complexity: Time O(n) amortised - each node is visited once by the outer walk, plus the walks to the child tails · Space O(1), the links are moved in place
files.input_note: Braces hold the child list of the value just before them, and may be nested: node 3 owns `7 8 9 10`, and node 8 inside it owns `11 12`.
files.output_note: `forward:  1 2 3 7 8 11 12 9 10 4 5 6` and `backward: 6 5 4 10 9 12 11 8 7 3 2 1` - the backward line is the exact reverse, which is the proof that every `prev` was fixed.
files.watch_out: Three links are easy to forget: `cur->child = NULL`, `childHead->prev = cur`, and the `prev` of the node that follows the child chain (guard it, because that node may be `NULL` at the end of a level).

check.q: Why is one walk enough even when a child list has its own children?
check.a: After splicing, `cur` steps into the child chain, so the outer loop reaches those nodes later and does the same splice again.

files.title: LRU cache (practice)
files.what: A store that holds only `capacity` keys. `get` and `put` both count as using a key; when the store is full, the key that has been waiting longest since its last use is thrown out. A doubly linked list keeps the use order and a map finds any node at once.
steps: The list holds the keys newest-first. Two fake nodes, `head` and `tail`, sit at the ends so every unhook and every insert has a node on both sides and there is no "is this the head?" case.
`table` maps a key to its node, so a key is found without walking the list - this is the one place the module reaches for a map.
`remove_node` unhooks a node by joining its two neighbours; `insert_at_front` puts a node just after `head`, which is what "newest" means here.
`get(key)`: not in the map → -1. Otherwise unhook the node, put it at the front (a get is a use) and return its value.
`put(key, value)` on a known key only changes the value and moves the node to the front - nothing is created or dropped.

For a new key on a full store, the node just before the fake `tail` is the least recently used one: unhook it, erase it from the map and `delete` it. That erase is why each node also stores its own key.
`main` reads `capacity` and a command count, then lines like `put 1 1` and `get 1`, printing what each get returns.
files.complexity: Time O(1) on average for both `get` and `put` · Space O(capacity)
files.input:
2 9
put 1 1
put 2 2
get 1
put 3 3
get 2
put 4 4
get 1
get 3
get 4
files.input_note: Capacity 2 and 9 commands - LeetCode's own example written in this command form.
files.output_note: `1`, `-1`, `-1`, `3`, `4`. The `get 1` both answers 1 and makes key 1 the newest, so `put 3 3` drops key 2; `put 4 4` then drops key 1.
files.watch_out: Without the key inside the node you cannot erase the evicted entry from the map, and the map would keep growing with pointers to deleted nodes. Also remember that a `get` counts as a use: if it does not move the node, the wrong key is evicted later.

check.q: Why is the node just before the fake `tail` the one to throw out?
check.a: Every use moves a node to the front, so the node nearest the back is the one nobody has touched for the longest time.

practice_links.name: Flatten a Multilevel Doubly Linked List

recap: A doubly node has `next` and `prev`; set both to `NULL` in the constructor.
Every change must keep `A->next == B` and `B->prev == A` true.
Head and tail insert/delete are all O(1); any-index operations are O(n) because of the walk.
Reuse the head/tail functions for index 0 and the last index.
When the list becomes empty, set both `head` and `tail` to `NULL`.

check_yourself.q: Which operation gets faster when you move from a singly to a doubly linked list with a tail pointer?
check_yourself.a: Deleting the tail: O(n) becomes O(1).

check_yourself.q: How can you quickly test that all `prev` links are correct?
check_yourself.a: Print the list forward and backward; the backward line should be the exact reverse of the forward line.

check_yourself.q: What does a doubly linked list cost in exchange for these benefits?
check_yourself.a: An extra pointer in every node (more memory) and more links to update in every operation.

body: In Module 7 you hit a wall. To drop the last node of `10 20 30 40` you had to start at the head and walk all the way to 30, just to set one pointer. The list knew where 40 was; it had no idea what sat behind it.

Picture a line of people where each person has been told only the name of the person in front. Ask the last one "who is behind you?" and they cannot answer. Ask them to leave, and somebody has to walk from the front to find the person who must now close the gap.
The fix is simple: give each person the name of the one behind them as well. In a node that is a second pointer, `prev`, beside the `next` you already have.
The chain now has arrows in both directions. `head->prev` is `NULL` because nothing comes before the first node, and `tail->next` is `NULL` because nothing comes after the last one:

One rule holds the whole thing together: **if `A->next` is `B`, then `B->prev` must be `A`.** Every insert and every delete has to fix both directions, not one. That is the new idea of this module, and also the new way to get it wrong.

There is a free test for it. Print the list from `head` following `next`, then from `tail` following `prev`. The second line must be the exact reverse of the first. If it is not, some `prev` was left behind. `print_doubly_link_list.cpp` on this page does just that, and prints `10 20 30` then `30 20 10`.
intro.trace:
head                        tail
 |                           |
 v                           v
NULL <- [10] <-> [20] <-> [30] -> NULL

body: **What the second arrow buys you.** Walking backwards is now an ordinary loop: start at `tail`, follow `prev` until `NULL`. In Module 6 the same job needed recursion, because there was no way to step back.

Deleting the tail drops from n steps to one. `tail->prev` *is* the second-last node, so `tail = tail->prev; tail->next = NULL;` and free the old one. On a list of 1000 nodes that is 999 steps saved every time.
And you no longer have to stand one node before the victim. Standing on the node itself is enough, because it can see both neighbours and introduce them to each other.
**An insert in the middle, arrow by arrow.** Put 200 after the 20 in `10 20 30 100 100`. You are standing on 20 as `tmp`, and four links change — two forward, two backward:

The order matters more than it looks. Set `tmp->next->prev` *before* you overwrite `tmp->next`. Once `tmp->next` points at the new node, 30 is no longer reachable from `tmp`, and you cannot fix its `prev` any more.

The head and tail inserts are the same idea with one neighbour missing, so `insert_at_any_position_doubly_linked_list.cpp` checks for `pos == 0` and for the end of the list first and calls those versions.
intro.snippet:
newNode->next = tmp->next;   // 200 -> 30
tmp->next->prev = newNode;   // 200 <- 30
tmp->next = newNode;         // 20  -> 200
newNode->prev = tmp;         // 20  <- 200

body: **And what it costs, plainly.** Every node now carries an extra pointer. On a typical 64-bit machine that is 8 more bytes per node, so a node holding a single `int` grows from roughly 16 bytes to roughly 24. If you never walk backwards and never delete from the end, you are paying for nothing.

The second cost is bugs. Every operation touches twice as many links, and a forgotten `prev` does not announce itself: the forward print still looks perfect, only the backward one disagrees. Emptying the list now means setting **both** `head` and `tail` to `NULL`.

The programs below build a doubly linked list by hand, print it both ways, then insert and delete at the head, the tail and any index. Several are broken on purpose — an uninitialised link that prints for ever, a `return;` where a `break;` belonged, a tail check that looks one node too close — and each note says which line to look at.
